claims.claim: The rocks move across the desert floor by themselves, without animal intervention
claims.quote: Sailing stones ... are part of the geological phenomenon in which rocks move and inscribe long tracks along a smooth valley floor without animal intervention.

claims.claim: Nothing pushes the stones
claims.quote: These thin, floating ice panels, frozen during cold winter nights, are driven by light winds, and shove rocks at up to 5 m/min

claims.claim: Trails run up to 330 feet (100 m) long
claims.quote: Tracks are often up to 330 ft (100 m) long, about 8 to 30 cm (3 to 12 in) wide, and typically much less than 2.5 cm (1 in) deep.

claims.claim: Trails are 3 to 12 inches wide and usually less than an inch deep
claims.quote: about 8 to 30 cm (3 to 12 in) wide, and typically much less than 2.5 cm (1 in) deep

claims.claim: The tracks have been studied since the early 1900s
claims.quote: At Racetrack Playa, these tracks have been studied since the early 1900s

claims.quote: Date: 23 August 2003 (18 October 2004 (original upload date)) Author: Jon Sullivan (pdphoto.org) / CC0 Licence: Public domain

claims.claim: Two rocks starting side by side may travel parallel and then one abruptly turns left
claims.quote: Rocks that start next to each other may travel parallel for a time, before one abruptly changes direction to the left, right, or even back to the direction from which it came.

claims.claim: Rough-bottomed stones cut straight striated tracks while smooth-bottomed ones wander
claims.quote: Stones with rough bottoms leave straight striated tracks, while those with smooth bottoms tend to wander.

claims.claim: Some stones flip over mid-journey
claims.quote: Stones sometimes turn over, exposing another edge to the ground and leaving a different track in the stone's wake.

claims.claim: A 2.5-inch stone travelled 860 feet
claims.quote: At 6.4 cm (2.5 in) in diameter, Nancy (stone H) was the smallest monitored stone. It also moved the longest cumulative distance, 260 m (860 ft)

claims.claim: Nancy moved 201 m (659 ft) in a single winter
claims.quote: and the greatest single winter movement, 201 m (659 ft)

claims.claim: Sharp and Carey tagged 30 rocks in 1968 and monitored them for seven years
claims.quote: Bob Sharp and Dwight Carey started a Racetrack stone movement monitoring program in May 1968. Eventually, 30 stones with fresh tracks were labeled and stakes were used to mark their locations. Each stone was given a name and changes in the stones' positions were recorded over a seven-year period.

claims.claim: All but two of the monitored stones moved
claims.quote: In the end, all but two of the monitored stones moved during the seven-year study.

claims.claim: "Nancy" moved the farthest of the monitored stones
claims.quote: It also moved the longest cumulative distance, 260 m (860 ft)

claims.claim: Nancy was the smallest of the monitored stones
claims.quote: At 6.4 cm (2.5 in) in diameter, Nancy (stone H) was the smallest monitored stone.

claims.claim: Karen is an estimated 700-pound block of dolomite
claims.quote: Karen (stone J) is a 74-by-48-by-51-centimeter (29 by 19 by 20 in) block of dolomite and weighs an estimated 320 kg (700 lb).

claims.claim: Karen never moved during the monitoring study
claims.quote: Karen did not move during the monitoring period.

claims.claim: Karen vanished from the playa before May 1994
claims.quote: However, Karen disappeared sometime before May 1994, possibly during the unusually wet winter of 1992 to 1993.

claims.claim: A geologist rediscovered Karen in 1996
claims.quote: Karen was rediscovered by San Jose geologist Paula Messina in 1996.

claims.claim: The movement is caused by thin ice sheets shoving the rocks during sunny mornings
claims.quote: Instead, rocks move when large ice sheets a few millimeters thick floating in an ephemeral winter pond start to break up during sunny mornings.

claims.claim: On 20 December 2013 more than 60 rocks were documented moving, at up to 5 m/min
claims.quote: The largest rock movement the research team witnessed and documented was on December 20, 2013, and involved more than 60 rocks

claims.claim: Rock movements were observed using GPS and time-lapse photography
claims.quote: News articles reported the mystery solved when researchers observed rock movements using GPS and time-lapse photography.

claims.claim: The ice sheets are only a few millimetres thick, frozen on a shallow winter pond, and are pushed by light winds
claims.quote: These thin, floating ice panels, frozen during cold winter nights, are driven by light winds, and shove rocks at up to 5 m/min

claims.claim: Some observed moves lasted 16 minutes
claims.quote: Some GPS-measured moves lasted up to 16 minutes

claims.claim: The observations ruled out the older idea of strong (90 mph) gusts dragging rocks through mud
claims.quote: These observations contradicted earlier hypotheses of strong winds or thick ice floating rocks off the surface.

claims.claim: Winter storm gusts on the playa can reach 90 mph
claims.quote: which can reach 140 km/h (90 mph) in winter storms

claims.claim: Rock movement requires a flooded playa and freezing nights
claims.quote: Because rock movement relies on a rare set of circumstances, the usually dry playa being flooded and the water freezing, drier winters and warmer winter nights would cause such circumstances to occur less often.

claims.claim: A statistical study by Ralph Lorenz and Brian Jackson suggests, at 4:1 odds, a decline in rock movement since the 1960s–90s
claims.quote: A statistical study by Ralph Lorenz and Brian Jackson examining published reports of rock movements suggested (with 4:1 odds) an apparent decline between the 1960s–1990s, and the 21st century.

claims.claim: Rocks have been stolen from the playa
claims.quote: On May 30, 2013, the Los Angeles Times reported that park officials were looking into the theft of several of the rocks from the Death Valley National Park.

claims.claim: In 2016 someone left 10 miles of tire tracks across the playa
claims.quote: In August 2016, around 10 miles (16 km) of tire tracks were left in the playa by someone driving around it illegally.

claims.claim: The vandal was still unidentified in 2018
claims.quote: the vandal had not been identified in March 2018

claims.claim: The first documented account of the phenomenon is from 1915, by a prospector named Joseph Crook of Fallon, Nevada
claims.quote: The first documented account of the sliding rock phenomenon dates to 1915, when a prospector named Joseph Crook from Fallon, Nevada, visited the Racetrack Playa site.
